name: Femi Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm lead hand for a small roofing and joinery firm in a seaside town, mostly houses and holiday flats. I cut roofs, which means I work out all the angles for the rafters and build them on site, plus dormers, repairs after storms, that kind of thing. Best feeling in the world is standing on a ridge at eight in the morning with the sea behind you and a roof that's square. Worst is February, wind off the water and wet timber, and you still have to be careful up there.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who do you work with, and who's at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My boss is Gary, he started the firm thirty years ago and still climbs ladders at sixty-two. There's three of us under him and I'm the one he leaves in charge. At home it's Ruth, she's a receptionist at the dental practice on the front, and our two, Joy's twelve and Kofi's nine. We've got a mortgage and, to be straight, about three weeks of money in the account, because holiday towns don't pay builders much in winter.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use AI in your work at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A bit. I've got an app that measures a roof from a photo, which I check with a tape, because it was out by a hand's width once. Sometimes I ask a chatbot what the rules say about something, like how big a window in a loft has to be for a fire exit. I started using it after the young lad at the timber yard showed me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it was oversold, like most things. At work I'd say the app's handy and leave it at that. I wouldn't post anything, I'm not that sort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means things stay as they are, which is fine for the job and not great for the money. Winters are tight and they'd still be tight. AI was never going to fix February.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as now and keep using the roof app and the chatbot when they're useful. I'd keep doing a few storm repairs at weekends for cash in the winter, same as I already do. Nothing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty normal, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a tight winter look like at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It looks like Ruth doing the shopping list with a calculator and me picking up every storm job going. Last January I did four Saturdays on the trot fixing slipped tiles. I've made more money from bad weather than from good, which tells you something about this town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has the app or the chatbot changed how you work so far?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. It saves me climbing up to measure for a quote, so I can price three jobs in a morning instead of one. Gary still wants me to go up and look before we start, and he's right.

S0.say: I'd say fair enough, AI was oversold like most things, and the roof app is handy. I wouldn't post anything about it.
S0.think: I think things stay the same, which suits the work but not the money. Winters would still be tight because AI was never going to fix February.
S0.do: Carries on as now, using the roof-measuring app and the chatbot when helpful. Keeps taking weekend storm repairs for extra cash in winter.
S0.quote: I've made more money from bad weather than from good, which tells you something about this town.
S0.fieldNote: Femi treats AI as a handy extra, checking it against his tape measure. The plateau leaves him calm because his main struggle is seasonal work in a holiday town. He already earns side money from storm repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's good and bad in it and we'll have to see. At work I'd tell the lads to learn the tools that work and not waste time on the ones that don't. Gary would say he's too old for it and I'd say no you're not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think roofs are near the back of the queue, because every old roof is different and you're working at height in the wind. But the measuring and pricing side, that's going to be done by computer. If quoting gets that easy, more firms will come in and undercut us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a bit to see what the bigger firms along the coast use, then copy whatever works. I'd learn the new tools properly once they're proven, and I'd start putting fifty a month away while work's still steady. I'd keep the weekend repairs going as a backstop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like watching the clouds over the headland.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned other firms undercutting you. Who's the worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a big outfit from the city that does holiday flats in bulk. If they can price a roof from a satellite picture, they'll take the easy work. We'd be left with the jobs nobody wants, the leaky old cottages, at the same price as before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Gary do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary would want to keep going the old way until he retires, which is about three years off. Then the question is whether he sells, or hands it to me, or just shuts it. I've never asked him straight.

S1.say: I'd say there's good and bad and we'll have to see. I'd tell colleagues to learn the tools that work and skip the ones that don't.
S1.think: I think roofs come late because each old roof is different and the work is at height in the wind. But pricing by computer could let bigger firms undercut us.
S1.do: Watches what bigger coastal firms adopt and copies what works. Learns proven tools, saves about fifty a month and keeps weekend repairs going.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like clouds gathering over the headland.
S1.quote: We'd be left with the jobs nobody wants, the leaky old cottages, at the same price as before.
S1.fieldNote: Femi's worry here is competition rather than robots: easier quoting helps bigger firms. He's a classic 'copy what works' adopter. A larger unknown lurks beneath: what happens when his boss retires.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast and somebody should have slowed it down, but I don't know who. I'd say to the lads, keep your heads, we'll work it out. People would be shouting at each other online and I'd stay out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it frightens me. If a robot can climb a roof by 2028, I've got two years of work left and three weeks of savings. There's no other roofing firm in town that would take me on, and the holiday trade is all I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Ruth and cut back hard straight away, no new school uniforms unless they're needed, no takeaway, sell the second car. I'd take every weekend repair job I could get, to build up even two months of cash. I'd ask the young lad at the timber yard to show me how the new machines work, in case someone needs a person to run them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. I'd lie awake listening to the wind and thinking about the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask how to run the machines. Does running them feel like a real option in two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe one in ten of us gets that job. There won't be a queue of robots needing a bloke from a seaside town to babysit them, will there? But I'd rather be in that queue than not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Joy and Kofi?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them Dad's still working, which would be true for a while. Joy would ask questions, she's twelve and sharp. Kofi would just want to know if we can still go to the cinema in the summer.

S2.say: I'd say this is too fast and someone should have slowed it down, though I don't know who. I'd tell my crew to keep calm and stay out of online shouting.
S2.think: I think it frightens me: two years of work left, three weeks of savings and no other roofing firm in town. The holiday trade is all I know.
S2.do: Cuts spending hard with Ruth and sells the second car. Takes every weekend repair job to build two months of cash and asks a younger contact to teach him the new machines.
S2.feel: Scared, lying awake listening to the wind and thinking about the mortgage.
S2.quote: There won't be a queue of robots needing a bloke from a seaside town to babysit them, will there?
S2.fieldNote: Femi doesn't know who to blame, which fits his middle-ground outlook. His plan mixes cost cutting, cash jobs and a long-shot bid to run machines. He's honest that very few people like him would get that job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if we're sensible. I'd tell the lads and Gary to start thinking now. I wouldn't go on about it, just get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years lines up with Gary retiring. If I could take over the firm and bring in a robot or two, I might come out alright, but I've got no money to buy anything. More likely the firm closes and I'm looking for work at forty-eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd ask Gary straight about his plans, which I've been putting off. I'd save every month, and once I saw which roofing robots actually worked on other sites, I'd train on them, maybe through the college in the city. I'd keep weekend jobs going the whole time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But it's the kind of anxious that gets you up and doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Gary, if you asked him straight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Gary, what happens to this place when you stop? I've been his right hand for eleven years and I've never had the nerve to ask if I'm in his plans. It's daft, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Training at the city college means travel and time. How would that work with the family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd be one evening a week and some Saturdays, and Ruth would have to cover the kids. She'd do it, she's done more for less. I'd lose some weekend repair money, so we'd have to plan the months around it.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if people are sensible. I'd tell my crew and boss to start thinking now and get on with it quietly.
S3.think: I think five years lines up with my boss retiring, so I might take over the firm with a robot or two, though I have no money. More likely it closes and I'm job hunting in my late forties.
S3.do: Asks Gary directly about his retirement plans in the first year. Saves monthly, trains on proven roofing robots at the city college, and keeps weekend jobs going.
S3.feel: Anxious in a way that pushes him to act.
S3.quote: I've been his right hand for eleven years and I've never had the nerve to ask if I'm in his plans.
S3.fieldNote: Five years makes Femi face a question he's been avoiding: his boss's succession. He can picture owning the business but has no money to make it happen. His training plan is realistic about the cost to family time and weekend income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for most of us to sort something out. I'd tell people not to panic and not to ignore it either. That's about as far as I'd go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years makes me feel a lot better. I'd be fifty-three, Joy and Kofi would be grown or close to it, and I could plan a change instead of being thrown into one. I'd still need to work, the mortgage won't be done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give it a couple of years to see what's real, then train in something next to roofing, like inspecting roofs and solar panels, because someone has to sign them off. I'd save steadily and talk to the kids about what they study. I wouldn't change jobs until the new one was solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can live with it. It's like a long forecast, you just plan around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why inspecting? What makes that safer, in your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because when a roof leaks, the owner wants someone to blame, and you can't sue a robot. Somebody with a name and a phone number has to put their signature on it. That could be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Joy about her studies?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She wants to be a vet, which I think is a good one, you need hands and a calm voice. I'd tell her go for it. I'd just ask her to have a second plan, which is what I wish someone told me.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough time for most people to sort something out. I'd tell people not to panic and not to ignore it.
S4.think: I think ten years makes me feel much better, at fifty-three with grown or nearly grown children. I could plan a change rather than be thrown into one, though I'd still need to work.
S4.do: Waits a couple of years to see what's real, then trains in roof and solar panel inspection. Saves steadily and talks with his children about their studies.
S4.feel: Uneasy but able to plan around it, like a long forecast.
S4.quote: Somebody with a name and a phone number has to put their signature on it.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years turns Femi from frightened to methodical, and he picks inspection because someone must sign off and be accountable. He wants proof before switching, true to his steady nature. His advice to his daughter is about having a fallback, which echoes his own regret.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. What would help is some kind of bridge, money to keep the mortgage paid while you retrain, and courses near home, not three hours away in the city.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the holiday towns. Places like ours live on summer and fix things in winter, and if robots do the fixing, I don't know what the winter is for.

headlineQuote: Places like ours live on summer and fix things in winter, and if robots do the fixing, I don't know what the winter is for.
portrait: Femi Santos is a 43-year-old roofing carpenter and lead hand for a small firm in a seaside town, with two kids, a partner who works at a dental practice, a mortgage and about three weeks of savings. He uses a roof-measuring app and a chatbot now and then, always checking them against his own work. He's calm about the plateau and uneasy that easier pricing could help bigger firms undercut his. AGI in two years alarms him and sends him scrambling for weekend cash. With five years he faces his boss's retirement, and with ten he plans a move into roof and solar inspection once he sees what's real.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he'd have two years of work left, three weeks of savings and no other roofing firm in town.
whatWouldHelp: A bridge payment to keep the mortgage paid while retraining, and courses close to home rather than in the city.
